analysis.one_liner: Bans most lawsuits against gun makers and sellers for harm caused by criminal misuse of their products.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 65-31 and the House 283-144 in 2005, and it became law on October 26, giving the firearms industry broad immunity from suits over crimes committed with its products.
analysis.plain_summary: This law blocks anyone from suing a gun or ammunition manufacturer, dealer, or importer in state or federal court for damages, injunctions, or penalties caused by the criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm. It also immediately dismisses lawsuits already in court when it was signed. A few narrow exceptions remain, such as suits over defective design, negligent handing of a gun to someone likely to misuse it, or knowing violations of sales laws, but a criminal discharge counts as the sole cause of the harm, sharply limiting defect claims. The law also requires a secure storage device with each handgun sold and adds a 15-year prison penalty for using armor-piercing ammunition in a violent or drug crime.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, importers, and their trade associations gain near-total protection from civil liability for harms caused when their products are criminally misused. Pending suits against them are thrown out. Gun owners benefit indirectly if liability fears would have raised prices or cut supply, and handgun buyers get a safety lock with each purchase.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun makers, sellers, and their trade groups

how_it_helps.text: Bars suits against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, and trade associations for damages, injunctions, fines, or penalties resulting from criminal or unlawful misuse of their products, and requires pending such suits to be dismissed.
Keeps narrow exceptions, including suits over defective design or manufacture, negligent entrustment, knowing violations of sales or marketing statutes, and breach of contract or warranty.

Adds the Child Safety Lock Act, requiring licensed dealers to include a secure gun storage or safety device with each handgun transferred, with license suspension or a civil penalty of up to $2,500 for violations.
Adds a mandatory 15-year prison term, on top of any sentence for the underlying crime, for using or carrying armor-piercing ammunition during a violent or drug trafficking crime.

analysis.who_pays: Victims of shootings and their families lose the ability to sue the seller or manufacturer when the harm came from criminal misuse, even in many cases where the product was defectively designed. Cities and plaintiffs with pending suits see them dismissed. The exceptions are narrow: once a discharge was a criminal act, that act is deemed the sole cause, effectively wiping out defect claims in shooting cases.

drawbacks.text: A discharge caused by a volitional criminal act is deemed the sole proximate cause of any harm, so product-defect claims are largely foreclosed in shooting cases even when the gun worked in a dangerously unexpected way.
Pending lawsuits were immediately dismissed, cutting off claims by victims and municipalities that had already filed.

Supporters acknowledged the point of the bill was to stop litigation they saw as an attempt to hold an entire industry liable for harm caused by others and to use courts to regulate firearms where legislatures had not.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argued it is unfair to sue makers of a lawful, heavily regulated product for crimes committed by someone else, and the bill does preserve narrow suits over defects, negligent entrustment, and knowing illegal sales. But the sole-proximate-cause rule and the dismissal of pending cases shift the cost of gun crimes onto victims and taxpayers, and no other consumer industry holds comparable immunity. The safety-lock and armor-piercing-ammo provisions are real but modest offsets.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate 65-31 in July 2005, passed the House 283-144 under a closed rule in October, and was signed by the President, becoming Public Law 109-92 on October 26, 2005.

narrative.text: The Senate ended debate on taking up the bill with a 66-32 cloture vote on July 26, 2005, then passed it with amendments 65-31 on July 29.
The House passed the Senate version without amendment 283-144 on October 20, 2005, under a rule that closed the bill to amendments.
It was signed by the President on October 26, 2005 and became Public Law 109-92.

The law protects manufacturers, sellers, importers, and trade associations from suits arising from criminal or unlawful misuse of firearms or ammunition and dismisses pending suits, while carving out narrow exceptions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The firearms industry and its trade associations gained a legal shield no other consumer industry has; victims' pending suits were wiped out and future ones barred. The president and the large bipartisan majorities that voted for it also got the policy outcome they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers, sellers, and trade associations

sides.party_line_note: Republicans backed it near unanimously (50-2 in the Senate, 223-4 in the House), while Democrats were divided but leaned against (14-29 in the Senate, 59-140 in the House).

industries.industry: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers
industries.note: The law gives them near-total immunity from civil suits over criminal or unlawful misuse of their products and dismisses pending suits, while their gain comes directly at the cost of victims' ability to recover. Narrow exceptions for defects, negligent entrustment, and knowing illegal sales remain but are limited by the sole-proximate-cause rule for criminal discharges.
Trade associations of gun makers and sellers are named beneficiaries of the suit ban, protecting groups such as the industry's chief lobbying organizations from liability actions.
Dealers must include a secure gun storage or safety device with each handgun sold, and owners who use one gain immunity from suits if a third party accesses the secured gun.
